# How do I know a result is real?

*You'll need fill models (chapter 6) and informed traders (chapter 5). From machine learning you'll need nothing new:
this is the chapter where your background transfers most directly.*

## The story

Prosperity 4's round 4 showed teams the names of the bots behind each trade, "Mark 14", "Mark 22", "Mark 67" and so
on, and every team went looking for an Olivia (chapter 5). Several found one. They didn't agree: one team's write-up
names Mark 67, another Marks 14 and 55, another 14 and 38
[(`references/wiki/contradictions.md`, row 3)]{.src}.

Ryan Challman's team fitted a weight for each named trader on the training days and used them to lean their fair
value. On the day they had held out, the weights turned out to be tuned to particular days' behaviour; switching them
off recovered about 15.8 thousand of held-out profit (*their claim*)
[(`references/prosperity4-ryan-challman/README.md:89-91`)]{.src}.

We ran the test that settles it: for each named trader, product and side, choose on two days, score on the third,
three times. No Mark that traded more than a handful of times a day kept the sign of its move on all three days and beat half the spread. Names chosen on two days by
their average move lost 31 thousand on the third. The careful teams were right to switch them off
[(`references/wiki/contradictions.md`, row 3)]{.src}.

Every one of those signals looked real on the days it was found on. That is the problem this chapter is about.

## The idea

### A grid is a hyperparameter search, with very few folds

A grid runs every combination of a few settings and ranks them. You know what happens next: the best of many noisy
estimates is biased upward, the winner's curse, and the more combinations, the bigger the bias. What is unusual here
is how little data there is. A Prosperity round gives three days; the Arena may give a handful. Three days are three
folds, they are correlated, and the scored day may come from a different regime.

So the repo never ranks by one number. Every grid prints, for each cell:

- **`pnl`**, profit, the total over all days;
- **`min day`**, its worst day, because a setting that wins on average by winning big once is fragile;
- **`nbhd`**, the neighbourhood, the average over the cell and its neighbours, because a lone spike among poor neighbours is luck;
- **PnL under a second fill model**, usually `worse`, because chapter 6.

A setting near the top on all four is worth more than the single best `pnl`.

### Hold out days, not ticks

The honest split is by day (@fig-folds): choose on two days, score on the third, and repeat for each day. Splitting
ticks at random would put a scored tick between two training ticks that share its price level and its regime, and
every method would look good.

![Leave one day out against shuffled k-fold. Days are the unit that can differ; ticks within a day share their
regime.](../figures/f11_folds.png){#fig-folds
fig-alt="Left: three rows of three day blocks, each row scoring a different day and fitting on the other two. Right: three rows of many thin tick blocks, scored and fitted ticks interleaved."}

### Statistics for "the best of many"

Held-out days answer "does the choice survive a day it wasn't made on". Four more tests, each printed by `arena.grid`,
answer "would the best of this many settings look this good by luck":

- **PBO, the probability of backtest overfitting** (Bailey et al., Definition 2.2, PDF p. 10). Cut the days into
  blocks, split the blocks into two halves in many ways (4,000 of the 48,620 possible
  halvings in the example below), pick the best cell on one half, and see where it ranks
  on the other:

  ::: {.eq speak="the probability of backtest overfitting is how often the best setting on one half of the data ranks below the median on the other half"}
  $$\text{PBO} = \Pr\big(\text{the in-sample best ranks below the median out of sample}\big)$$
  :::

  Near 0 is good; 50% means choosing was no better than picking at random.
- **DSR, the deflated Sharpe ratio** (a Sharpe ratio is the mean gain over its standard deviation): is the best
  cell's risk-adjusted gain larger than the best of that many cells
  with no gain would show?
- **SPA and StepM:** bootstrap tests of whether any cell, and then which cells, beat the bot as it is (its current
  settings), accounting for
  every cell tried. StepM's list at 4% is what the repo trusts.
- **The permutation test** (chapters 5 and 6): run the whole search on days with their ticks shuffled. If it finds as good
  a best, the choice doesn't need anything that happens over time.

### One grid, read in full

@fig-grid is Kelp's two edges on Prosperity 3's round 1, under both fill models: `make_edge`, how far from the fair
the bot quotes, and `take_edge`, how far the book must be mispriced before it takes.

![Kelp's `make_edge` against `take_edge` on Prosperity 3's round 1, PnL over three days (both products; only Kelp's
settings change), under `all` and `worse`. Data: `data/kelp_grid.csv`, from `arena.grid ... --modes all,worse`.](../figures/f10_kelp_grid.png){#fig-grid
fig-alt="Two heat maps of profit over make edge and take edge. Under all, the best cell is make edge 1.5, take edge 1, at 84.5 thousand. Under worse, the best is make edge 0, take edge 0.5, at 63.9 thousand, and the cells at make edge 1.5 and above are among the worst."}

Under `all` the case for quoting wider looks strong. The best cell, `make_edge` 1.5 with `take_edge` 1, is best by
total, by worst day and by neighbourhood; it is chosen on every held-out day; PBO is 0%; SPA says some cell beats the
bot as is (a p-value of 0.000) and StepM names nine. Only the DSR hesitates (0.74, under its 0.95 bar).

Then the second fill model. Under `worse`, only one of StepM's nine cells beats the bot as is, by 596. The repo's
rule, the *pick*, takes StepM's best cell that beats the bot as is under every mode, and here that is a small step,
`make_edge` 0.5 with `take_edge` 0.5: +736 under `all`, +596 under `worse`. Every statistic was right about the data it
saw. None of them could see that the data was replayed under an assumption
[(the grid's own output, from `data/kelp_grid.csv`'s command)]{.src}.

### When the profit is on one day

One more failure the tests don't catch: concentration. Ryan Challman's `ROBOT_DISHES` made about 389 thousand on one
training day against 11 thousand and 4 thousand on the other two, 96% on one day; its mean reversion was strong on
that day only. Rather than tune to that day, they halved its weight, a hedge against the scored day not looking like it
(*their claim*) [(`references/prosperity4-ryan-challman/README.md:115-141`)]{.src}. The `min day` column and the held-out days
are there to show you such a profile before you size to it.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
Everything here is model selection under multiple comparisons, and the tools are the ones you know: held-out folds,
corrections for the number of trials, permutation nulls. Three things are harsher than usual. There are three folds,
not a thousand. The folds are correlated and the test day may come from another distribution. And the simulator that
scores every fold shares one bias (chapter 6), which no statistic computed inside it can detect, so the second fill
model is part of the validation, not an extra.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="In the repo"}
- `uv run python -m arena.grid BOT DAYS --grid PARAMS.P.key=v1,v2 --modes all,worse [--holdout last] [--permute 19]`:
  every measure above, the held-out days, PBO, DSR, SPA, StepM and the `pick` (`python/arena/grid.py`,
  `python/arena/stats.py`).
- The rows: "A permutation test of the whole search", "Selection rules on unseen days", "Following informed
  counterparties".
:::

::: {.callout-important title="On the day"}
`RUNBOOK.md`, "Each round", T+1:00: the grid under two fill models, and a setting changes only to the summary's
`pick`, with the one exception RUNBOOK names for round 1 if the rounds are scored on raw PnL.
:::
